{{Short description|Distance function defined between probability distributions}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Wasserstein distance''' or '''[[Leonid Kantorovich|Kantorovich]]–[[Gennadii Rubinstein|Rubinstein]] metric''' is a [[metric (mathematics)|distance function]] defined between [[Probability distribution|probability distributions]] on a given [[metric space]] <math>M</math>. It is named after [[Leonid Vaserstein|Leonid Vaseršteĭn]].

Intuitively, if each distribution is viewed as a unit amount of earth (soil) piled on ''<math>M</math>'', the metric is the minimum "cost" of turning one pile into the other, which is assumed to be the amount of earth that needs to be moved times the mean distance it has to be moved.  This problem was first formalised by [[Gaspard Monge]] in 1781.  Because of this analogy, the metric is known in [[computer science]] as the [[earth mover's distance]].

==Definition==

Let <math>(M,d)</math> be a [[metric space]] that is a [[Polish_space#Radon_spaces|Polish space]]. For <math>p \in [1, +\infty]</math>, the Wasserstein <math>p</math>-distance between two [[probability measure]]s <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> on <math>M</math> with finite <math>p</math>-[[Moment (mathematics)|moments]] is
:<math>W_p(\mu, \nu) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu)} \left(\mathbf{E}_{(x, y) \sim \gamma} d(x, y)^p \right)^\frac{1}{p},</math>
where <math>\Gamma(\mu, \nu)</math> is the set of all [[coupling (probability)|couplings]] of <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math>; <math>W_\infty(\mu, \nu)</math> is defined to be
:<math>\lim_{p\rightarrow +\infty} W_p(\mu, \nu)</math>
and corresponds to a [[supremum norm]]. Here, a coupling <math>\gamma</math> is a [[joint probability]] measure on <math>M \times M</math> whose [[marginal distribution|marginals]] are <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> on the first and second factors, respectively. This means that for all measurable <math>A\subset M</math>, it fulfills
<math>\gamma(A\times M) = \mu(A)</math> and
<math>\gamma(M\times A) = \nu(A)</math>.

The case of <math>p = \infty</math> is special:<math display="block">
  W_{\infty}(\mu,\nu) = \lim_{p \rightarrow +\infty} W_p(\mu,\nu) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu) } \gamma\operatorname{-essup} d(x,y),
</math>where <math>\gamma\operatorname{-essup} d(x,y)</math> denotes the [[essential supremum]] of <math>d(x,y)</math> with respect to measure <math>\gamma</math>. The metric space ('''''P'''''<sub>∞</sub>(''M''), ''W''<sub>∞</sub>) is complete if (''M'',&nbsp;''d'') is separable and complete. Here, '''''P'''''<sub>∞</sub> is the space of all probability measures with bounded support.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Givens |first1=Clark R |last2=Shortt |first2=Rae Michael |date=1984 |title=A class of Wasserstein metrics for probability distributions. |journal=Michigan Mathematical Journal |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=231–240 |doi=10.1307/mmj/1029003026 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Naming ===
The name "Wasserstein distance" was coined by [[Roland Dobrushin|R. L. Dobrushin]] in 1970, after learning of it in the work of [[Leonid Vaserstein|Leonid Vaseršteĭn]] on Markov processes describing large systems of automata<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Vaserstein LN |year=1969 |title=Markov processes over denumerable products of spaces, describing large systems of automata |url=http://www.mathnet.ru/links/b90e28ab49fa878b215cbbdfa0235264/ppi1811.pdf |journal=Problemy Peredači Informacii |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=64–72}}</ref> (Russian, 1969). However the metric was first defined by [[Leonid Kantorovich]] in ''The Mathematical Method of Production Planning and Organization''<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kantorovich LV |year=1939 |title=Mathematical Methods of Organizing and Planning Production |journal=Management Science |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=366–422 |doi=10.1287/mnsc.6.4.366 |jstor=2627082}}</ref> (Russian original 1939) in the context of optimal transport planning of goods and materials. Some scholars thus encourage use of the terms "Kantorovich metric" and "Kantorovich distance". Most [[English language|English]]-language publications use the [[German language|German]] spelling "Wasserstein" (attributed to the name "Vaseršteĭn" ({{langx|ru|Васерштейн}}) being of [[Yiddish]] origin).

==Intuition and connection to optimal transport==
[[File:Transport-plan.svg|thumb|Two one-dimensional distributions <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math>, plotted on the <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> axes, and one possible joint distribution that defines a transport plan between them. The joint distribution/transport plan is not unique]]
One way to understand the above definition is to consider the [[optimal transport problem]]. That is, for a distribution of mass <math>\mu(x)</math> on a space <math>X</math>, we wish to transport the mass in such a way that it is transformed into the distribution <math>\nu(x)</math> on the same space; transforming the 'pile of earth' <math>\mu</math> to the pile <math>\nu</math>. This problem only makes sense if the pile to be created has the same mass as the pile to be moved; therefore [[without loss of generality]] assume that <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> are probability distributions containing a total mass of 1. Assume also that there is given some cost function

<math display="block">c(x,y) \geq 0</math>

that gives the cost of transporting a unit mass from the point <math>x</math> to the point <math>y</math>.
A transport plan to move <math>\mu</math> into <math>\nu</math> can be described by a function <math>\gamma(x,y)</math> which gives the amount of mass to move from <math>x</math> to <math>y</math>. You can imagine the task as the need to move a pile of earth of shape <math>\mu</math> to the hole in the ground of shape <math>\nu</math> such that at the end, both the pile of earth and the hole in the ground completely vanish. In order for this plan to be meaningful, it must satisfy the following properties:

<ol><li>the amount of earth moved out of point <math>x</math> must equal the amount that was there to begin with; that is,

<math display="block">\int \gamma(x,y) \,\mathrm{d} y = \mu(x),</math>

and</li>
<li>the amount of earth moved into point <math>y</math> must equal the depth of the hole that was there at the beginning; that is,

<math display="block">\int \gamma(x,y) \,\mathrm{d} x = \nu(y).</math>
</li></ol>

That is, that the total mass moved ''out of'' an infinitesimal region around <math>x</math> must be equal to <math>\mu(x) \mathrm{d}x</math> and the total mass moved ''into'' a region around <math>y</math> must be <math>\nu(y)\mathrm{d}y</math>. This is equivalent to the requirement that <math>\gamma</math> be a [[joint probability distribution]] with marginals <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math>. Thus, the infinitesimal mass transported from <math>x</math> to <math>y</math> is <math>\gamma(x,y) \, \mathrm{d} x \, \mathrm{d} y</math>, and the cost of moving is <math>c(x,y) \gamma(x,y) \, \mathrm{d} x \, \mathrm{d} y</math>, following the definition of the cost function. Therefore, the total cost of a transport plan <math>\gamma</math> is
<math display="block">
\iint c(x,y) \gamma(x,y) \, \mathrm{d} x \, \mathrm{d} y = \int c(x,y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma(x,y).
</math>

The plan <math>\gamma</math> is not unique; the optimal transport plan is the plan with the minimal cost out of all possible transport plans. As mentioned, the requirement for a plan to be valid is that it is a joint distribution with marginals <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math>; letting <math>\Gamma</math> denote the set of all such measures as in the first section, the cost of the optimal plan is
<math display="block">
C =  \inf_{\gamma \in \Gamma(\mu, \nu)} \int c(x,y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma(x,y).
</math>
If the cost of a move is simply the distance between the two points, then the optimal cost is identical to the definition of the <math>W_1</math> distance.

=== Fortification ===
[[Gaspard Monge]], who first considered the problem, considered it as an abstraction of a practical problem. Monge studied [[descriptive geometry]] in the context of [[military fortification]]. At the time, the outer walls were built with a large amount of earth which would be costly to transport. Furthermore, the ground near the outer walls would also be shaped with structures like [[Ditch|ditches]] to remove favorable attacking positions. The military engineer, during design, should design it according to the terrain, so that for each sector of the fortress, the volume of the ''déblai'' (the earth excavated) would approximately equal the ''remblai'' (the material which built up the body of the rampart).<ref>{{cite book |last=Duffy |first=Christopher |title=Fire and Stone: The Science of Fortress Warfare 1660–1860 |date=2006-01-01 |publisher=Castle |isbn=978-0785821090 |location=London |pages=44-49 |language=en}}</ref>

Monge abstracted the problem of minimizing transport cost between the ''déblai'' and ''remblai'' into a problem in pure geometry, and published it as ''Mémoire sur la Théorie des Déblais et des Remblais''.

==Examples==

=== Point masses ===

Point masses naturally arise in statistics. If <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are [[Empirical distribution function|empirical distributions]], each based on <math>n</math> observations, then<math display="block">W_p(P, Q) =  \inf_\pi \left( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \|X_i - Y_{\pi(i)}\|^p \right)^\frac{1}{p},</math>where the infimum is over all permutations <math>\pi</math> of <math>n</math> elements. This is a [[linear assignment problem]], and can be solved by the [[Hungarian algorithm]] in [[cubic time]].

===Normal distributions===

Let <math>\mu_1 = \mathcal{N}(m_1, C_1)</math> and <math>\mu_2 = \mathcal{N}(m_2, C_2)</math> be two non-degenerate [[Gaussian measure]]s (i.e. [[normal distribution]]s) on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, with respective [[expected value]]s <math>m_1</math> and <math>m_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n</math> and [[symmetric positive definite|symmetric positive semi-definite]] [[covariance matrix|covariance matrices]] <math>C_{1}</math> and <math>C_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}</math>.  Then,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Olkin I, Pukelsheim F | title = The distance between two random vectors with given dispersion matrices | journal = Linear Algebra and Its Applications | volume = 48 | date = October 1982 | pages = 257–263 | issn = 0024-3795 | doi = 10.1016/0024-3795(82)90112-4 | doi-access = free }}</ref> with respect to the usual Euclidean norm on <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>, the 2-Wasserstein distance between <math>\mu_{1}</math> and <math>\mu_{2}</math> is
<math display="block">W_{2} (\mu_1, \mu_2)^2 = \| m_1 - m_2 \|_2^2 + \mathop{\mathrm{trace}} \left( C_1 + C_2 - 2 \left( C_2^\frac12 C_1 C_2^\frac12 \right)^\frac12 \right) .</math>
where <math>C^\frac12</math> denotes the [[Square root of a matrix#Positive semidefinite matrices|principal square root]] of <math>C</math>. Note that the second term (involving the trace) is precisely the (unnormalised) [[Bures metric]] between <math>C_1</math> and <math>C_2</math>.
This result generalises the earlier example of the Wasserstein distance between two point masses (at least in the case <math>p = 2</math>), since a point mass can be regarded as a normal distribution with covariance matrix equal to zero, in which case the [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] term disappears and only the term involving the Euclidean distance between the means remains.

===One-dimensional distributions===

Let <math>\mu_1, \mu_2 \in P_p(\mathbb{R})</math> be probability measures on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, and denote their [[cumulative distribution function|cumulative distribution functions]] by <math>F_1(x)</math> and <math>F_2(x)</math>. Then the transport problem has an analytic solution: Optimal transport preserves the order of probability mass elements, so the mass at quantile <math>q</math> of <math>\mu_1</math> moves to quantile <math>q</math> of <math>\mu_2</math>.
Thus, the <math>p</math>-Wasserstein distance between <math>\mu_1</math> and <math>\mu_2</math> is
<math display="block">W_p(\mu_1, \mu_2) = \left(\int_0^1 \left| F_1^{-1}(q) - F_2^{-1}(q) \right|^p \, \mathrm{d} q\right)^\frac{1}{p},</math>
where <math>F_1^{-1}</math> and <math>F_2^{-1}</math> are the [[quantile function|quantile functions]] (inverse CDFs).
In the case of <math>p=1</math>, a change of variables leads to the formula<ref>S. S. Vallander, Theory of Probability and its Applications, 1974, Volume 18, Issue 4, Pages 784–786
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1137/1118101</ref>
<math display="block">W_1(\mu_1, \mu_2) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left| F_1(x) - F_2(x) \right| \, \mathrm{d} x. </math>

==Properties==

===Metric structure===

''W''<sub>''p''</sub> satisfies all the [[axiom]]s of a [[metric (mathematics)|metric]] on the Wasserstein space '''''P'''''<sub>''p''</sub>(''M'') consisting of all Borel probability measures on ''M'' having finite ''p''th moment.

Convergence with respect to ''W''<sub>''p''</sub> is equivalent to the usual [[weak convergence of measures]] plus convergence of the first ''p''th moments.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Clement P, Desch W |title=An elementary proof of the triangle inequality for the Wasserstein metric|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|volume=136|number=1|year=2008|pages=333–339|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-07-09020-X|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/2008-136-01/S0002-9939-07-09020-X/home.html|doi-access=free}}</ref>

For any ''p'' ≥ 1, the metric space ('''''P'''''<sub>''p''</sub>(''M''), ''W''<sub>''p''</sub>) is [[Separable space|separable]], and is [[Complete space|complete]] if (''M'', ''d'') is separable and complete.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Bogachev VI, Kolesnikov AV |date=October 2012 |title=The Monge–Kantorovich problem: achievements, connections, and perspectives |journal=[[Russian Mathematical Surveys]] |volume=67 |issue=5 |pages=785–890 |bibcode=2012RuMaS..67..785B |doi=10.1070/RM2012v067n05ABEH004808 |s2cid=121411457}}
</ref>

=== Existence ===
By a theorem of Gangbo and McCann, if <math>X, Y</math> are subsets of <math>\R^n</math>, and the cost function <math>c(x, y) = h(x - y)</math> for some strictly convex function <math>h: \R^n \to \R</math>, then the optimal transport problem has a unique optimal transport map. In particular, for all <math>p > 1</math>, optimal transport map exists and is unique.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gangbo |first=Wilfrid |last2=McCann |first2=Robert J. |date=1996-09-01 |title=The geometry of optimal transportation |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02392620 |journal=Acta Mathematica |language=en |volume=177 |issue=2 |pages=113–161 |doi=10.1007/BF02392620 |issn=1871-2509}}</ref>

===Duality===
[[Leonid Kantorovich|Kantorovich]] and Rubinstein proved a duality representation theorem for general cost functions <math>c(x, y)</math>, of which the Wasserstein metric is a special case.

Given a cost function <math>c(x, y)</math>, it produces a duality transformation <math>\psi \mapsto \psi^c</math> defined by<math display="block">\psi^c(y) := \inf_x (c(x, y) - \psi(x)) </math>This generalizes [[Legendre transformation]], which is the case where <math>c(x, y) = xy</math> with a sign flip.

We say that a function <math>\psi</math> is '''''c''-convex''' iff <math>\psi = \varphi^c</math> for some <math>\varphi</math>. Like in the case of convex transformation, a function is ''c''-convex iff its double dual is itself. In this language, the '''Kantorovich duality''' states theorem:<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Villani |first=Cédric |author-link=Cédric Villani |title=Optimal Transport: Old and New |date=2009 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-71049-3 |editor-last=Berger |editor-first=M. |series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |editor-last2=Serre |editor-first2=D. |editor-last3=Sinaj |editor-first3=Jakov G. |editor-last4=Sloane |editor-first4=N. J. A. |editor-last5=Vershik |editor-first5=A. M. |editor-last6=Villani |editor-first6=Cédric |editor-last7=Waldschmidt |editor-first7=M. |editor-last8=Eckmann |editor-first8=B. |editor-last9=Harpe |editor-first9=P.}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Thm. 5.10}}<blockquote>If <math>(X, \mu_X), (Y, \mu_Y)</math> are [[Polish space|Polish probability spaces]], <math>c : X \times Y \to \R \cup\{\infty\}</math> is [[lower semicontinuous]], and there exists some upper semicontinuous functions <math>a \in L^1(\mu_X), b \in L^1(\mu_Y) </math> such that <math>c(x, y) \geq a(x) + b(y)</math>, then<math display="block">\inf_{\gamma \in \Gamma (\mu, \nu) } \left( \int_{X \times Y} c(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x, y) \right)
=
\sup_{\varphi \text{ is }c\text{-convex}} \left( \int_X \varphi (x) \, \mathrm{d} \mu (x) + \int_Y \varphi^c (y) \, \mathrm{d} \nu (y) \right)</math>If furthermore, <math>c</math> only takes real values, there exists a transport plan with finite cost, and there exists some functions <math>a' \in L^1(\mu_X), b' \in L^1(\mu_Y) </math> such that <math>c(x, y) \leq a'(x) + b'(y)</math>, then<math display="block">\min_{\gamma \in \Gamma (\mu, \nu) } \left( \int_{X \times Y} c(x, y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x, y) \right)
=
\max_{\varphi \text{ is }c\text{-convex}} \left( \int_X \varphi (x) \, \mathrm{d} \mu (x) + \int_Y \varphi^c (y) \, \mathrm{d} \nu (y) \right)</math></blockquote>

==== Proof ====
The following is an intuitive proof which skips over technical points. A fully rigorous proof is found in.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Villani |first=Cédric |title=Topics in optimal transportation |date=2003 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=0-8218-3312-X |location=Providence, RI |chapter=Chapter 1: The Kantorovich Duality |oclc=51477002}}</ref>

'''Discrete case''': When <math>M</math> is discrete, solving for the 1-Wasserstein distance is a problem in linear programming:
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
	  \min_\gamma \displaystyle \sum_{x, y} c(x, y) \gamma(x, y) \\[6pt]
	  \displaystyle \sum_y \gamma(x, y) = \mu(x) \\[6pt]
	  \displaystyle \sum_x \gamma(x, y) = \nu(y) \\[6pt]
	  \gamma \geq 0
	  \end{cases}
</math>
where <math>c: M \times M \to [0, \infty)</math> is a general "cost function".

By carefully writing the above equations as matrix equations, we obtain its [[Dual linear program|dual problem]]:<ref>{{Citation |last1=Matoušek |first1=Jiří |title=Understanding and Using Linear Programming |pages=81–104 |year=2007 |series=Universitext |chapter=Duality of Linear Programming |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-30717-4_6 |isbn=978-3-540-30697-9 |last2=Gärtner |first2=Bernd}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
	  \max_{f, g} \displaystyle \sum_x \mu(x)f(x) + \sum_y \nu(y)g(y)\\[6pt]
	  f(x) + g(y) \leq c(x, y)
	  \end{cases}
</math>
and by the [[Dual linear program#Strong duality|duality theorem of linear programming]], since the primal problem is feasible and bounded, so is the dual problem, and the minimum in the first problem equals the maximum in the second problem. That is, the problem pair exhibits ''strong duality''.

For the general case, the dual problem is found by converting sums to integrals:
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
	  \sup_{f, g} \mathbb E_{x\sim \mu}[f(x)] + \mathbb E_{y\sim \nu}[g(y)]\\[6pt]
	  f(x) + g(y) \leq c(x, y)
	  \end{cases}
</math>
and the ''strong duality'' still holds.
This is the '''Kantorovich duality theorem'''. [[Cédric Villani]] recounts the following interpretation from [[Luis Caffarelli]]:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Villani |first=Cédric |title=Topics in optimal transportation |date=2003 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=0-8218-3312-X |location=Providence, RI |chapter=1.1.3. The shipper's problem. |oclc=51477002}}</ref>
<blockquote>
Suppose you want to ship some coal from mines, distributed as <math>\mu</math>, to factories, distributed as <math>\nu</math>. The cost function of transport is <math>c</math>. Now a shipper comes and offers to do the transport for you. You would pay him <math>f(x)</math> per coal for loading the coal at <math>x</math>, and pay him <math>g(y)</math> per coal for unloading the coal at <math>y</math>.

For you to accept the deal, the price schedule must satisfy <math>f(x) + g(y) \leq c(x, y)</math>. The Kantorovich duality states that the shipper can make a price schedule that makes you pay almost as much as you would ship yourself.</blockquote>This result can be pressed further to yield:{{Math theorem
| math_statement = When the probability space <math>\Omega</math> is a metric space, then
<math display="block">W_1(\mu, \nu) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \leq 1} \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu}[f(x)] -\mathbb E_{y\sim \nu}[f(y)]</math>
where <math>\|\cdot\|_L</math> is the [[Lipschitz norm]].
| name = Theorem
| note = Kantorovich-Rubenstein duality
}}{{Math proof|proof= 
Start with
<math display="block">W_1(\mu, \nu) = \sup_{f(x) + g(y) \leq d(x, y)} \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu}[f(x)] +\mathbb E_{y\sim \nu}[g(y)].</math>
Then, for any choice of <math>g</math>, one can push the term higher by setting <math>f(x) = \inf_y d(x, y) - g(y)</math>, making it an [[infimal convolution]] of <math>-g</math> with a cone. This implies <math>f(x) - f(y) \leq d(x, y)</math> for any <math>x, y</math>, that is, <math>\|f\|_L \leq 1</math>.

Thus,
<math display="block">\begin{align}
			  W_1(\mu, \nu) &= \sup_{g}\sup_{f(x) + g(y) \leq d(x, y)} \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu}[f(x)] +\mathbb E_{y\sim \nu}[g(y)]\\[6pt]
			  &= \sup_{g}\sup_{\|f\|_L \leq 1, f(x) + g(y) \leq d(x, y)} \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu}[f(x)] +\mathbb E_{y\sim \nu}[g(y)]\\[6pt]
			  &= \sup_{\|f\|_L \leq 1}\sup_{g, f(x) + g(y) \leq d(x, y)} \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu}[f(x)] +\mathbb E_{y\sim \nu}[g(y)].
			  \end{align}
</math>
Next, for any choice of <math>\|f\|_L\leq 1</math>, <math>g</math> can be optimized by setting <math>g(y) = \inf_x d(x, y) - f(x)</math>. Since <math>\|f\|_L\leq 1</math>, this implies <math>g(y) = -f(y)</math>.
}}

[[File:Infimal_convolution_of_a_cone_with_a_cubic_curve.svg|thumb|Infimal convolution of a cone with a curve. Note how the lower envelope has slope <math>\leq 1</math>, and how the lower envelope is ''equal'' to the curve on the parts where the curve itself has slope <math>\leq 1</math>.]] The two infimal convolution steps are visually clear when the probability space is <math>\R</math>.

For notational convenience, let <math>\square</math> denote the infimal convolution operation.

For the first step, where we used <math>f = \text{cone} \mathbin{\square} (-g)</math>, plot out the curve of <math>-g</math>, then at each point, draw a cone of slope 1, and take the lower envelope of the cones as <math>f</math>, as shown in the diagram, then <math>f</math> cannot increase with slope larger than 1. Thus all its secants have slope <math>\bigg| \frac{f(x) - f(y)}{x-y}\bigg| \leq 1</math>.

For the second step, picture the infimal convolution <math>\text{cone} \mathbin{\square} (-f)</math>, then if all secants of <math>f</math> have slope at most 1, then the lower envelope of <math>\text{cone} \mathbin{\square} (-f) </math> are just the cone-apices themselves, thus <math>\text{cone} \mathbin{\square} (-f)=-f</math>.

'''1D Example'''. When both <math>\mu, \nu</math> are distributions on <math>\R</math>, then [[integration by parts]] give
<math display="block">\mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu}[f(x)] - \mathbb E_{y\sim \nu}[f(y)] = \int f'(x) (F_\nu(x) - F_\mu(x)) \, \mathrm{d}x,</math>
thus
<math display="block">f(x) = K \cdot \operatorname{sign}(F_\nu(x) - F_\mu(x)).</math>

== ''W''<sub>1</sub> ==
In the case of ''W''<sub>1</sub>, we have <math>c(x, y) = d(x, y)</math>, and there is a particularly simple way to state that a function is c-convex in this case: a function <math>f</math> is ''c''-convex iff it is Lipschitz, with [[Lipschitz constant]] <math>\leq 1</math>. In this case, <math>f^c = -f</math>, so the Kantorovich duality states that<math display="block">W_1 (\mu, \nu) = \sup \left\{ \left. \int_{M} f(x) \, \mathrm{d} (\mu - \nu) (x) \, \right| \text{ continuous } f : M \to \mathbb{R}, \operatorname{Lip} (f) \leq 1 \right\},</math>This form shows that ''W''<sub>1</sub> is an [[integral probability metric]]. If there exists a <math>f</math> that reaches the supremum exactly, then such a function is called a '''Kantorovich potential''' for this optimal transport problem.

For example, for any <math>k > 2</math>, the optimal transport plan of moving an upside-down unit hemisphere centered at <math>(0, 0, k)</math> to a rightside-up unit hemisphere centered at <math>(0, 0, 0)</math> is simply moving it along the ''z''-direction. This is proven by using the Kantorovich potential <math>f(x, y, z) = z</math>.

=== Connection to Radon measure ===
Compare this with the definition of the [[Radon metric]]:<math display="block">\rho (\mu, \nu) := \sup \left\{ \left. \int_M f(x) \, \mathrm{d} (\mu - \nu) (x) \, \right| \text{ continuous } f : M \to [-1, 1] \right\}.</math>If the metric ''d'' of the metric space (''M'',''d'') is bounded by some constant ''C'', then<math display="block">2 W_1 (\mu, \nu) \leq C \rho (\mu, \nu),</math>and so convergence in the Radon metric (identical to '''total variation convergence''' when ''M'' is a [[Polish space]]) implies convergence in the Wasserstein metric, but not vice versa.

=== Geometric interpretation ===
Monge's original insight was that, in the case where <math>X</math> is a Riemannian manifold with the geodesic distance metric, the duality of optimal transport is geometrically meaningful.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Cayley |first=Arthur |author-link=Arthur Cayley |date=November 1882 |title=On Monge's “Mémoire sur la Théorie des Déblais et des Remblais.” |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1112/plms/s1-14.1.139 |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=s1-14 |issue=1 |pages=139–143 |doi=10.1112/plms/s1-14.1.139}}</ref>

Let <math>\gamma</math> be an optimal transport plan from <math>\mu</math> to <math>\nu</math>. To avoid complications and make the imagery clear, suppose that <math>\gamma</math> is a ''deterministic'' plan. That is, it is equivalent to a transport ''map'' <math>T: \operatorname{supp}(\mu) \to \operatorname{supp}(\nu)</math>, so that any infinitesimal lump of coal at <math>x</math> is transported to <math>T(x)</math>. The entire transport map can then be drawn as a family of geodesic curve segments in <math>X</math> connecting each <math>x</math> to its corresponding <math>T(x)</math>. These are '''transport rays'''.

Monge noted that the transport rays do not intersect at an angle, because otherwise the plan is not optimal. Concretely, suppose that there exist <math>x, x'</math> such that <math>x \to T(x)</math> and <math>x' \to T(x')</math> intersect at an X-shape at some point <math>y</math>, then we can redirect <math>x</math> to <math>T(x')</math> and vice versa, and "pull apart" the X-shape into a )(-shape, and thus cost less in transport. Therefore, the transport rays make up a non-intersecting family of geodesic arcs.

==== Planar case ====
[[File:Monge caustic for a circle and a line segment.webm|thumb|Let <math>\mu</math> be the uniform distribution on the unit circle, and <math>\nu</math> on a unit line segment. The line congruence produces a caustic curve, and the involutes of the caustic curve are the contours of the Kantorovich potential field.]]
Monge studied first the case where <math>X = \R^2</math>, in which case transport rays are line segments. He studied in particular the case where the transport rays cover a solid region of the plane. That is, we have a 1-parameter family of lines, a '''[[Pseudosphere#Line congruence|line congruence]]'''. He showed that these are orthogonal to a 1-parameter family of curves. That is, there exists some partially defined <math>f: \R^2 \to \R</math>, such that each contour curve <math>f^{-1}(k)</math> is orthogonal to the transport rays, and furthermore, the curves are separated by their distance. That is, starting on some point <math>z</math> on the curve <math>f^{-1}(k)</math>, and move along the transport ray that the point <math>z</math> is on for a distance <math>\delta k</math>, we would arrive at a point on the curve <math>f^{-1}(k + \delta k)</math>. This is the Kantorovich potential.

Any point in the thin slice can be moved to any other point in the other thin slice without changing the cost. All such plans are optimal. Furthermore, any other plan is suboptimal. In this way, the Kantorovich potential field entirely solves the problem.
[[File:Kantorovich potential from a line to a line plus a point.svg|thumb|Let <math>\mu</math> be the uniform distribution on the line segment <math>(0, 0) \to (0, 1)</math>, and <math>\nu</math> have two parts: half on a point mass at <math>(1, 0)</math>, and half uniform on the line segment <math>(-1, 0) \to (-1, 2)</math>. The contours of the Kantorovich potential field is plotted.]]
Each line in the line congruence divides the plane into two halves, such that the mass of <math>\mu, \nu</math> in the two halves are the same. The line congruence produces a caustic curve, and the involutes of the caustic curve are the contours of the Kantorovich potential field.

==== Spatial case ====
Next, Monge noted that when <math>X = \R^3</math>, transport rays are line segments. He studied in particular the case where the transport rays cover a solid region of space. That is, we have a 2-parameter line congruence. He showed that these are orthogonal to a 1-parameter family of surfaces. That is, there exists some partially defined <math>f: \R^3 \to \R</math>, such that each contour surface <math>f^{-1}(k)</math> is orthogonal to the transport rays, and furthermore, the surfaces are separated by their distance. That is, starting on some point <math>z</math> on the surface <math>f^{-1}(k)</math>, and move along the transport ray that the point <math>z</math> is on for a distance <math>\delta k</math>, we would arrive at a point on the surface <math>f^{-1}(k + \delta k)</math>. This is the Kantorovich potential.

Any infinitesimal circle in the transport rays sweeps out a thin tube in space, and it encloses one thin filament in <math>\mu</math> and another in <math>\nu</math>. Any point in one thin filament can slide along the tube to any other point in the other thin filament without changing the cost. All such plans are optimal. Furthermore, any other plan is suboptimal. In this way, the Kantorovich potential field entirely solves the problem.[[File:Standard_contact_structure.svg|right|thumb|The standard contact structure on <math>\R^3</math>.]]
Unlike the planar case, a non-intersecting family of line congruences cannot in general be normal to any surface. For example, consider the standard [[contact structure]] on <math>\R^3</math>, which can be understood as a field of infinitesimal planes. Now, perpendicular to every infinitesimal plane, draw a directed ray. This gives us a "twisted" line congruence. There is no surface perpendicular to the congruence, because there is no surface that can be tangent to every infinitesimal plane.

However, Monge showed that in this particular case, this 2-parameter line congruence can be split into a 1-parameter family of 1-parameter line congruences, in such a way that each such 1-parameter line congruence is a [[developable surface]]. In fact, there are two ways to split. Thus, the 2-parameter line congruence is generated as the grid of intersections between two 1-parameter families of developable surfaces. He showed that a line congruence satisfying such a condition ''is'' normal to a 1-parameter family of surfaces, and thus he constructed the surfaces. In modern language, he showed that this is an ''[[Integrable system|integrable]]'' [[foliation]] of space by lines.

Each contour surface <math>f^{-1}(k)</math> intersects these two families of developable surfaces at two families of curves, and Monge named them "[[lines of curvature]]". He would later study those of the [[ellipsoid]] in 1795. Let the surfaces be contours of the equation <math>f(x, y, z) = const</math>. The lines of curvature can be computed from the equation, and 4 lines of curvature produce an infinitesimal square tube. The volumes of <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> cut by the square tube are equal. This is the [[partial differential equation]] satisfied by the surface.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="EB1911">{{cite EB1911|wstitle=Monge, Gaspard|author=Arthur Cayley|author-link=Arthur Cayley|volume=18|pages=709–710}}</ref>

==== General case ====
In general, at each point <math>z</math> on a transport ray <math>x \to T(x)</math>, define the unit velocity vector <math>v_z</math>. This produces a [[vector field]]. The vector field cannot have curl in it, since if there is a curl, then effectively, some lump of coal is being transported in a cycle, which is suboptimal. Therefore, the vector field is [[Conservative vector field|irrotational]], thus locally integrable as the gradient field <math>\nabla f</math> of some function <math>X \to\R</math>. This corresponds to the general fact that an optimal transport plan is [[Cyclical monotonicity|''c''-cyclically monotonic]]. In this way, an optimal transport map produces the Kantorovich potential.

Note that in general, the Kantorovich potential is not everywhere differentiable, and there may be singular points on its surface. For example, consider the transport from the unit circle in <math>\R^2</math> to the origin. Its optimal transport rays are radii of the circle, and its Kantorovich potential has a sharp point at origin. However, it is still differentiable [[Generic property|generically]], i.e. almost everywhere (like in [[Sard's theorem]]).

Conversely, given a continuous <math>f : X \to \R</math> such that almost everywhere it is differentiable with gradient <math>\nabla f</math> of unit length, it is a Kantorovich potential, and its gradient flow generates an optimal transport map.

This duality between the transport ''rays'' and the potential ''field'' can be regarded as a [[Huygens–Fresnel principle]].

=== Economic interpretation ===
Economically, this can be interpreted as follows. Consider a market of coals. The price of coal vary over space, so define the price function <math>f: X \to \R</math>, where <math>f(x)</math> is the price of coal at location <math>x</math>.

The market may have opportunity for spatial [[arbitrage]], means that <math>\exists x, x' \in X</math> such that <math>f(x) - f(x') > d(x, x')</math>. An enterprising merchant can then buy coal at <math>x'</math> and sell coal at <math>x</math>, earning a net profit of <math>f(x) - f(x') - d(x, x')</math>.

The price function is ''c''-convex iff it is free of spatial arbitrage. For example, a market of constant pricing <math>f = c_0</math> has no spatial arbitrage, since the coal is the same price everywhere, so any movement of coal would waste transportation without earning any profit.

Given such a market, a configuration of coal <math>\mu</math> has a total market-value of <math>\int_X f d\mu</math>, and two configurations <math>\mu, \nu</math> may have differing market-values <math>\int_X f d(\mu - \nu)</math>. The two parts of duality then state:

* <math>W_1(\mu, \nu) \geq \int_X f d(\mu - \nu)
 </math> for any arbitrage-free market pricing, because otherwise, one can purchase <math>\nu </math>, transport to <math>\mu </math> using an optimal transport plan at a cost of <math>W_1(\mu, \nu) </math>, then sell it, creating profit, so <math>f </math> is not arbitrage-free after all.
* In the case of exact equality <math>W_1(\mu, \nu) = \int_X f d(\mu - \nu)
 </math>, the price <math>f </math> can be interpreted as the [[shadow price]] of any optimal transport plan, and any transport plan that exactly breaks even is an optimal plan.

The shadow price interpretation is Kantorovich's original understanding of the duality between optimal planning and market pricing.

== ''W''<sub>2</sub> ==

=== Monge–Ampère equation ===
Suppose <math>\mu, \nu</math> are distributions on <math>\R^n</math> with probability density functions <math>\rho_\mu, \rho_\nu</math>. In this case, a map <math>T : \operatorname{supp}(\mu) \to \operatorname{supp}(\nu)</math> is a transport map iff it satisfies<math display="block">\int h(T(x)) \rho_\mu(x) dx = \int h(y) \rho_\nu(y) dy</math>for any integrable test function <math>h \in L^1(\operatorname{supp}(\nu))</math>.

By a theorem of Brenier, the optimal transport map is the (almost everywhere) unique gradient of a convex function <math>u: \operatorname{supp}(\mu) \to \R^n</math>, with <math>T = \nabla \psi</math>. The convex function satisfies a [[Monge–Ampère equation]]:<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=282}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Prins |first=C. R. |last2=Beltman |first2=R. |last3=ten Thije Boonkkamp |first3=J. H. M. |last4=IJzerman |first4=W. L. |last5=Tukker |first5=T. W. |date=January 2015 |title=A Least-Squares Method for Optimal Transport Using the Monge--Ampère Equation |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/140986414 |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |language=en |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=B937–B961 |doi=10.1137/140986414 |issn=1064-8275}}</ref><math display="block">\begin{cases}
\det(\nabla^2 \psi) = \frac{\rho_\mu}{\rho_\nu \circ \nabla \psi}\\
\nabla \psi(\partial\operatorname{supp}(\mu)) = \partial \operatorname{supp}(\nu)
\end{cases}</math>The boundary condition simply states that the optimal transport maps the boundary of the source to the boundary of the target.

Conversely, some Monge–Ampère equations can be interpreted optimal transport. Weak-solutions of a Monge–Ampère equations obtained by optimal transport are often called '''Brenier solutions''' in the literature. Brenier solutions satisfy their corresponding Monge–Ampère equations almost everywhere.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=323}}

This connection to the Monge–Ampère equation allows one to apply [[regularity theory]] to optimal transport with quadratic cost.

==== Applications to geometry ====
At this point, a very short proof of the [[Isoperimetric inequality|'''isoperimetric inequality''']] appears.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Figalli |first=Alessio |title=The Monge-Ampère equation and its applications |date=2017 |publisher=European Mathematical Society |isbn=978-3-03719-170-5 |series=Zurich lectures in advanced mathematics |location=Zürich}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Sec. 4.2.6}} The inequality states that among all open sets of <math>\R^n</math> with smooth boundaries, the sphere has the smallest surface area (after scaling). That is,<math display="block">|\partial X| \geq n |B_1|^{1/n} |X|^{1-1/n}</math>for any open subset <math>X \subset \R^n</math> with smooth boundary.

Consider the quadratic cost transport problem from the uniform distribution on <math>X</math> to the uniform distribution on <math>B_1</math>. By the regularity theory of optimal transport, there exists some convex <math>u</math>, smooth on all of <math>X</math>, such that <math>T: X \to B_1</math> defined by <math>T = \nabla u</math> is a transport map. (Note that we don't need the optimality of <math>T</math>, just its existence.)

Then we have the following properties:<math display="block">\begin{cases}
|T| \leq 1 \\ 
\det(DT) = \frac{|B_1|}{X} \\
\operatorname{div} (T) \geq n \det(DT)^{1/n}
\end{cases}</math>The first two properties are because <math>T</math> is a transport map. The third property is by first noting that the convexity of <math>u</math> implies all eigenvalues of <math>DT</math> are nonnegative, then applying the [[AM–GM inequality]]. This then gives<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
|\partial X | &= \int_{\partial X} dS \geq  \int_{\partial X} |T| dS \\
&\geq\int_{\partial X} (T \cdot \hat n) dS = \int_X \operatorname{div}(T) dV \\
&\geq  \int_X n \det(DT)^{1/n} dV = n|B_1|^{1/n}|X|^{1-1/n} 
\end{aligned}</math>Here we use the notation commonly used in [[vector calculus]] in 3 dimensions, though it works in any dimension.

=== Minimizing flow ===
Angenent, Haker, and Tannenbaum proposed a way to obtain the optimal transport map by minimizing flow.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Angenent |first=Sigurd |last2=Haker |first2=Steven |last3=Tannenbaum |first3=Allen |date=January 2003 |title=Minimizing Flows for the Monge--Kantorovich Problem |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0036141002410927 |journal=SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis |language=en |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=61–97 |doi=10.1137/S0036141002410927 |issn=0036-1410}}</ref>

=== Fluid mechanics interpretation ===
Benamou & Brenier found a dual representation of <math>W_2</math> by [[fluid mechanics]], which allows efficient solution by [[convex optimization]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benamou |first1=Jean-David |last2=Brenier |first2=Yann |date=2000-01-01 |title=A computational fluid mechanics solution to the Monge-Kantorovich mass transfer problem |journal=Numerische Mathematik |language=en |volume=84 |issue=3 |pages=375–393 |doi=10.1007/s002110050002 |s2cid=1100384 |issn=0945-3245}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Finlay |first1=Chris |last2=Jacobsen |first2=Joern-Henrik |last3=Nurbekyan |first3=Levon |last4=Oberman |first4=Adam |date=2020-11-21 |title=How to Train Your Neural ODE: the World of Jacobian and Kinetic Regularization |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/finlay20a.html |journal=International Conference on Machine Learning |language=en |publisher=PMLR |pages=3154–3164|arxiv=2002.02798 }}</ref>

Given two probability densities <math>p, q</math> on <math>\R^n</math>,
<math display="block">W_2^2(p, q)=\min_{\bold{v}} \int_0^1 \int_{\R^n} \|\bold{v}(\bold{x}, t)\|^2 \rho(\bold{x}, t) \, d \bold{x} \, dt</math>
where <math>\bold{v}</math> ranges over velocity fields driving the [[continuity equation]] with boundary conditions on the fluid density field:
<math display="block">
\dot{\rho}+\nabla\cdot(\rho\bold{v})=0 \quad
\rho(\cdot, 0)=p,\; \rho(\cdot, 1)=q
</math>
That is, the mass should be conserved, and the velocity field should transport the probability distribution <math>p</math> to <math>q</math> during the time interval <math>[0, 1]</math>.

===Negative-order Sobolev norm===

Under suitable assumptions, <math>W_2</math> is Lipschitz-equivalent to a negative-order homogeneous [[Sobolev space|Sobolev norm]]. More precisely, if we take <math>M</math> to be a [[connected space|connected]] [[Riemannian manifold]] equipped with a positive measure <math>\pi</math>, then we may define for <math>f \colon M \to \mathbb{R}</math> the seminorm
<math display="block">\| f \|_{\dot{H}^{1}(\pi)}^{2} = \int_{M} \|\nabla f(x)\|^{2} \, \pi(\mathrm{d} x)</math>
and for a [[signed measure]] <math>\mu</math> on <math>M</math> the dual norm
<math display="block">\| \mu \|_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\pi)} = \sup \bigg\{ | \langle f, \mu \rangle | \,\bigg|\, \| f \|_{\dot{H}^{1}(\pi)} \leq 1 \bigg\} .</math>
Then any two probability measures <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> on <math>M</math> satisfy the upper bound <ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Peyre R | title = Comparison between ''W''<sub>2</sub> distance and ''H&#775;''<sup>&minus;1</sup> norm, and localization of Wasserstein distance | journal = ESAIM: Control, Optimisation and Calculus of Variations | volume = 24 | date = October 2018 | issue = 4 | pages = 1489–1501 | issn = 1292-8119 | doi = 10.1051/cocv/2017050 | doi-access = free }} (See Theorem 2.1.)</ref>
<math display="block">W_{2} (\mu, \nu) \leq 2\, \| \mu - \nu \|_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\pi)} .</math>
In the other direction, if <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> each have densities with respect to the [[volume form|standard volume measure]] on <math>M</math> that are both bounded above by some <math>0 < C < \infty</math>, and <math>M</math> has non-negative [[Ricci curvature]], then <ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Loeper G | title = Uniqueness of the solution to the Vlasov–Poisson system with bounded density | journal = Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées | volume = 86 | date = July 2006 | issue = 1 | pages = 68–79 | issn = 1292-8119 | doi = 10.1016/j.matpur.2006.01.005 | doi-access = free | arxiv = math/0504140 }} (See Theorem 2.9.)</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Peyre R | title = Comparison between ''W''<sub>2</sub> distance and ''H&#775;''<sup>&minus;1</sup> norm, and localization of Wasserstein distance | journal = ESAIM: Control, Optimisation and Calculus of Variations | volume = 24 | date = October 2018 | issue = 4 | pages = 1489–1501 | doi = 10.1051/cocv/2017050 | doi-access = free }} (See Theorem 2.5.)</ref>
<math display="block">\| \mu - \nu \|_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\pi)} \leq \sqrt{C}\, W_{2} (\mu, \nu) .</math>

=== Gradient flow ===

==Applications==

The Wasserstein metric is a natural way to compare the probability distributions of two variables ''X'' and ''Y'', where one variable is derived from the other by small, non-uniform perturbations (random or deterministic).

In computer science, for example, the metric ''W''<sub>1</sub> is widely used to compare discrete distributions, ''e.g.'' the [[color histogram]]s of two [[digital images]]; see [[earth mover's distance]] for more details.

In their paper '[[Wasserstein GAN]]', Arjovsky et al.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Arjovsky M, Chintala S, Bottou L |date=July 2017 |title=Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/arjovsky17a.html |journal=International Conference on Machine Learning 214-223 |pages=214–223}}</ref> use the Wasserstein-1 metric as a way to improve the original framework of [[generative adversarial network]]s (GAN), to alleviate the [[Vanishing gradient problem|vanishing gradient]] and the [[mode collapse]] issues. The special case of normal distributions is used in a [[Frechet inception distance]].

The Wasserstein metric has a formal link with [[Procrustes analysis]], with application to chirality measures,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Petitjean M |year=2002 |title=Chiral mixtures |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-02122882/file/PMP.JMP_2002.pdf |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |volume=43 |issue=8 |pages=4147–4157 |bibcode=2002JMP....43.4147P |doi=10.1063/1.1484559 |s2cid=85454709}}</ref> and to shape analysis.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Petitjean M |year=2004 |title=From shape similarity to shape complementarity: toward a docking theory |journal=Journal of Mathematical Chemistry |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=147–158 |doi=10.1023/B:JOMC.0000033252.59423.6b |s2cid=121320315}}</ref>

In applied and computational topology, the Wasserstein metric can be used to compare [[Persistent homology|persistence diagrams]], for example cytometry datasets in [[computational biology]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Mukherjee S, Wethington D, Dey TK, Das J |date=March 2022 |title=Determining clinically relevant features in cytometry data using persistent homology |journal=PLOS Computational Biology |volume=18 |issue=3 |arxiv=2203.06263 |bibcode=2022PLSCB..18E9931M |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009931 |pmc=9009779 |pmid=35312683 |doi-access=free |article-number=e1009931}}</ref>

The Wasserstein metric also has been used in inverse problems in geophysics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Frederick |first1=Christina |last2=Yang |first2=Yunan |date=2022-05-06 |title=Seeing through rock with help from optimal transport |url=https://publications.mfo.de/handle/mfo/3941 |journal=Snapshots of Modern Mathematics from Oberwolfach |doi=10.14760/SNAP-2022-004-EN}}</ref>

The Wasserstein metric is used in [[integrated information theory]] to compute the difference between concepts and conceptual structures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oizumi |first1=Masafumi |last2=Albantakis |first2=Larissa |last3=Tononi |first3=Giulio |date=2014-05-08 |title=From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0 |journal=PLOS Computational Biology |volume=10 |issue=5 |bibcode=2014PLSCB..10E3588O |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003588 |pmc=4014402 |pmid=24811198 |doi-access=free |article-number=e1003588}}</ref>

The Wasserstein metric and related formulations have also been used to provide a unified theory for shape observable analysis in high energy and collider physics datasets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ba |first1=Demba |last2=Dogra |first2=Akshunna S. |last3=Gambhir |first3=Rikab |last4=Tasissa |first4=Abiy |last5=Thaler |first5=Jesse |date=2023-06-29 |title=SHAPER: can you hear the shape of a jet? |journal=Journal of High Energy Physics |language=en |volume=2023 |issue=6 |page=195 |arxiv=2302.12266 |bibcode=2023JHEP...06..195B |doi=10.1007/JHEP06(2023)195 |issn=1029-8479 |s2cid=257205971}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-03-29 |title=Awards, fellowships and the shape of physics: News from the College {{!}} Imperial News {{!}} Imperial College London |url=https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/244052/awards-fellowships-shape-physics-news-from/ |access-date=2023-10-31 |website=Imperial News |language=en}}</ref>
